title: References and Pass by Reference
summary: Create aliases with references, let functions change the caller's variables, and pass big objects by const reference.
intro: Every parameter you have written so far was a copy. A reference is a second name for an existing variable, with no copy at all. It lets a function change the caller's data, and with `const` it lets a function read big objects without copying them.

steps.title: References are aliases
steps.body:
A reference is another name for an existing variable. Write `&` after the type and bind it when you declare it:

```cpp
int x = 5;
int& r = x;  // r and x name the same int
r += 1;      // x is now 6
int c = x;   // c is a separate int holding 6
```

No new memory is made for the value: `r` refers to the same bytes as `x`, so a change through either name shows through both. A copy like `c` gets its own memory and is independent from then on.

Two rules set references apart from ordinary variables:

- A reference must be initialized. `int& r;` does not compile.
- A reference cannot be re-bound. `r = y;` copies the value of `y` into `x`. It does not make `r` refer to `y`.

> Gotcha: `auto` drops the `&`. `auto c = r;` deduces `int` and makes a copy. Write `auto& c = r;` when you want another reference.

example.title: Score alias
example.prompt: Change a score through a reference, a copy, and two auto variables, and print which changes reach the original.
example.explanation: `alias` and `score` share one `int`, so adding 10 through `alias` shows up in both, while `copy` grew on its own to 55. `auto other = alias;` deduced a plain `int`, so `other` became 61 and `score` stayed 60. `auto& same` is a reference, so adding 1 through it moved `score` to 61. The last assignment did not re-bind `alias`: it copied 99 into `score`.

practice.title: City alias
practice.prompt:
Make a reference and a copy of a city name and see which changes reach the original.

1. Declare `std::string city = "Oslo";`, then `std::string& place = city;` and `std::string backup = city;`.
2. Append `" Norway"` through `place` and `"!"` through `backup`.
3. Print `city`, `place`, and `backup`, one per line.
4. Make `auto again = place;` and append `"?"` to it, then make `auto& same = place;` and append `"?"` to it.
5. Print `city` once more.

Expected output:

```text
Oslo Norway
Oslo Norway
Oslo!
Oslo Norway?
```

tests.output:
Oslo Norway
Oslo Norway
Oslo!
Oslo Norway?

hints: A reference is declared like `std::string& place = city;` and a copy like `std::string backup = city;`.
`auto again = place;` is a copy, so appending to it leaves `city` alone. Only `same` adds the `?` to `city`.

steps.title: Pass by value vs pass by reference
steps.body:
A plain parameter such as `int n` is a copy: the function gets its own `int` and the caller's variable never changes. Add `&` to make it a reference parameter. Now the parameter is another name for the caller's variable, and changes go straight back:

```cpp
void reset(int& n) {
    n = 0;  // changes the caller's variable
}
```

Nothing is copied: the function works on the caller's own bytes. So the argument must be a variable (or an element such as `v[i]`) of that type. `reset(5)` and `reset(a + b)` do not compile, because there is no variable for `n` to refer to.

Reference parameters also let a function hand back more than one result. The caller passes variables, and the function fills them in. These are called out-parameters:

```cpp
void minMax(int a, int b, int& lo, int& hi);
```

Out-parameters show how references work, but modern C++ prefers returning a value, a struct, or a pair. Returning a `std::vector` does not copy its elements either, as the Copy and Move lesson shows.

> Gotcha: never return a reference to a local variable. The local is gone when the function ends, so the reference dangles and using it is undefined behavior.

example.title: Bonus points and division
example.prompt: Add a bonus by copy and by reference, then return a quotient and remainder through out-parameters.
example.explanation: `addBonusCopy` added 10 to its own copy, which vanished when it returned, so `points` still printed 100. `addBonus` took `points` by reference, so its `+= 10` changed `main`'s variable to 110. `divide` wrote both results into `quotient` and `remainder` through its reference parameters, so one call produced two answers.

practice.title: Doubling and split time
practice.prompt:
Write functions that double a number by copy and by reference, then split a duration into minutes and seconds.

1. Write `void doubleCopy(int n)` that doubles `n`, and `void doubleIt(int& n)` that doubles `n`.
2. In `main`, starting from `int value = 21;`, call `doubleCopy(value)` and print `value`, then call `doubleIt(value)` and print `value`.
3. Write `void splitTime(int totalSeconds, int& minutes, int& seconds)` that fills in whole minutes and leftover seconds.
4. Call it with 754 and print the result as `12 min 34 s`.

Expected output:

```text
21
42
12 min 34 s
```
hints: Only `doubleIt` has `&` on its parameter, so only it changes `value`.
Declare `int minutes = 0;` and `int seconds = 0;` in `main` and pass them to `splitTime`.
Whole minutes are `totalSeconds / 60` and leftover seconds are `totalSeconds % 60`.

steps.title: const references: no copy, no changes
steps.body:
Passing a `std::vector` or `std::string` by value copies every element into new memory, which is slow for big data. A `const` reference gives the function the caller's object with no copy, and the `const` promises it will only read:

```cpp
int total(const std::vector<int>& values);
// values.push_back(1); inside total would not compile
```

The compiler rejects any change through a `const&`, so callers know their data is safe. It also accepts temporaries and literals, unlike a plain `&`.

Pick a parameter style with one rule:

| Parameter | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `int n`, `double x` | small types: copying is as cheap as a reference |
| `const std::string& s` | strings, containers, and objects you only read |
| `std::vector<int>& v` | anything the function must change |

Inside the function, loop with `for (const auto& x : v)` to read each element without copying it.

C++17 also has `std::string_view`, a cheap read-only view of text. It does not own the characters, so it must not outlive the string it views. This course sticks with `const std::string&`.

example.title: Team totals
example.prompt: Sum scores and print names through const references, and add a name through a plain reference.
example.explanation: `total` and `printAll` only read, so they take `const&` and work on the caller's vectors directly with no copy. `addName` must change `team`, so it takes a plain `&` for the vector and a `const&` for the new name. The literal `"Mia"` is fine there because a `const std::string&` can bind to a temporary string. `const auto& name` reads each string in place.

practice.title: Ratings and word lengths
practice.prompt:
Write read-only helpers that take a list of ratings and a list of words by const reference, plus one that changes the word list.

1. Write `double average(const std::vector<double>& xs)` that returns the mean, or `0.0` when `xs` is empty.
2. Write `int countLonger(const std::vector<std::string>& words, std::size_t minLength)` that counts words longer than `minLength`.
3. Write `void addWord(std::vector<std::string>& words, const std::string& word)` that appends `word`.
4. Print `Average: ` with the average of `ratings` (the starter sets 2 decimals) and `Longer than 4: ` with `countLonger(words, 4)`.
5. Call `addWord(words, "papaya")` and print `Longer than 4: ` with the new count.

Expected output:

```text
Average: 3.69
Longer than 4: 2
Longer than 4: 3
```
hints: Sum with `for (double x : xs)` and divide by `static_cast<double>(xs.size())`.
In `countLonger`, loop with `for (const auto& word : words)` and compare `word.size() > minLength`.
`addWord` needs a plain `&` on the vector because it changes it.

recap:
- `int& r = x;` makes `r` another name for `x`: same memory, no copy.
- A reference must be initialized and can never be re-bound. `r = y;` copies `y` into `x`.
- `auto c = r;` makes a copy, `auto& c = r;` makes another reference.
- A value parameter works on a copy. A `&` parameter changes the caller's variable and can serve as an out-parameter.
- Pass small types by value, strings, containers, and objects by `const&` to read, and by `&` only to modify.
- The compiler rejects changes through a `const&`, and `for (const auto& x : v)` reads elements without copying.
- Never return a reference to a local variable: it dangles.
